Jean Jacques Rousseau in his Letter to D'Alambert equates the protagonist of this play to himself and suggests a different ending. This work's last section "Fruit and Seed" ends by quoting four lines of Samson Agonisthes. One of this man's novels sees the ghost of Maeve Livingston avenge herself on her murderer, the cowardly Grahame Coats. Some of his comrades refer to him as the "Iron Mask," and George Pons mistakenly believes he is the author of "Junius." The Latin phrase that opens the second line of this poem's second stanza means "Hail to thee," whereas the nonsensical three words that end the sixth line in the ninth and final stanza begin a necromantic spell. The speaker also utters in Latin, "Hail, Virgin full of grace" denoting the beginning of the Vespers that call him away at the poem's end. The reference to "twenty-nine damnations" in the seventh stanza is from Deuteronomy not Galatians as the poem states. Among the sins the speaker ascribes are lusting after Sweet Dolores and Sanchicha, ostensibly two residents of the titular locale, who have been eyed by the speaker not Brother Lawrence to whom the speaker attributes his shortcomings. In this work, the title character threatens to leave after he is told that his speeches are too long, whereupon Hippias offers his services as a moderator. After going to the house of Callias, the title character explains his views in the form of an apologue, which describes how after Prometheus had given men the arts, Zeus is represented as sending Hermes to them, bearing with him Justice and Reverence. The title character views are also heavily discussed in the Theatetus, in that work Socrates claims that he holds that wind is cold to him who is cold, and not to him who is not. Introducing the notion that it is impossible to knowingly commit and evil act and setting out to show whether virtue can be taught, name this eponymous Socratic dialogue in which the titular sophist claims, "man is the measure of all things."

The protagonist of Jeffrey Archer's novel, A Prisoner of Birth, repeatedly compares his plight and his plan to that of the protagonist of this novel. Lesbian undertones characterize the relationship between Eugenie and her music teacher Louise, who by novel's end have run off to Rome, where we earlier met the bandit leader Luigi Vampa. The love of Valentine and Maximillian is solely heterosexual as is that of the protagonist for his young ward, the Turkish princess Haydee. The final part of the protagonist's plan sees the bankruptcy of Danglars come to fruition, which follows the ruination of both Villefort and Fernand, the other two figures involved in framing the protagonist in a Bonapartist plot. The Prologue to this work suggests that "When Anna's sceptre points the laws their course... There scarce is room for satire," and is spoken by Mr. Wilks. After kissing a maid named Cherry, one character compares her lips to honeycombs, to which she replies that she wishes there had been bees too, to sting him for his impudence. In this play, the highwayman Gibbet makes a plan to rob the household of a character who is flirting with the captive French officer Bellair, while Foigard is revealed to be an Irishman posing as a Frenchman in this play. The arrival of Sir Charles Freeman, who confirms the story of the death of the eldest brother of the two main characters, results in an inheritance for one of the main characters and the separation of Freeman's sister from her brutish husband. Ending with Archer engineering Mrs. Sullen's divorce from her husband and Aimwell's marriage to Dorinda, identify this late Restoration comedy, the most famous work of George Farquhar.

One of these works begins by telling of how its author was asked to write an introduction to a Leonard Merrick novel, and goes on, by way of Chesterton, to classify works such as the Sherlock Holmes stories as "good bad books." Another of these works analyzes the titular writer's new book The Machiavellians, and is a commentary on the author of The Managerial Revolution, James Burnham. Including works such as "The Lion and the Unicorn," which defends patriotic feelings towards the subtitular nation, as well as "In Defense of P.G. Wodehouse," among these works is one which compares Henry Miller to Walt Whitman in analyzing Miller's Tropic of Cancer and Black Spring. In addition to "Inside the Whale," another of these works condemns such artifices as dying metaphors, pretentious diction, and meaningless words in analyzing the titular tongue, while one of the most famous of these works admits that the title action was committed "solely to avoid looking a fool." Including such works as "Decline of the English Murder," and "Politics and the English Language," identify these non-fiction works by the author of "Shooting an Elephant," some of which are collected in Burmese Days.

In the foreword to this work, its author references a brief correspondence he had with Johan Bojer, who published a similar work shortly prior to this work's publication. After treating an Indian chief for blood poisoning, the main character of this work receives a pony as a reward, and a female character in this work recalls how her parents begged her husband not to take her across the sea, and laments the "west-fever" which she sees among the young. The naming of a boy who is jokingly prophesied to become President because, "he is born in the country," causes tension in this work between Kjersti and Tonseten. In this work's final chapter, entitled "The Great Plain Drinks the Blood of Christian Men and is Satisfied," the main character dies in a snowstorm while trying to get a minister for Hans Olsa, and his last thoughts are of his wife Beret and his son Peder Victorious. Identify this novel about Per Hansa, a Norwegian who settles in the Dakotas, the most famous work of Ole Rolvaag.

A poem in which this composer finds himself a prisoner on a ship during a mutiny was written by Thomas Transtromer about this composer's "dream." At his death, this composer left unfinished a piano concerto in E-flat major, which was completed by Lyapunov, who also conducted the first premiere of this composer's Second Symphony. The composer of a notoriously difficult "oriental fantasy," identify this member of the "mighty five," a teacher to Borodin, Rimsky-Korsakov, and Musorgsky and composer of Islamey.

This poem's fourth stanza contains a dubious attempt to rhyme "draught" with "quaffed," and in the foregoing stanzas, the title character dreams of her father wearing "a broadcloth coat," and her brother sailing "a painted boat." That character marries "a wife of richest dower/ Who lived for fashion as he for power," while this work's main character ends up married to "a man unlearned and poor/ And many children played round her door." At the beginning of Max Frisch's Homo Faber, a man identified only as a "ruin-lover" procures a Land Rover so the main character can visit this nation. The author of those aforementioned works, which includes the novel Mulatta, also authored a collection of legends of this country, and another work by that author centers of Miguel Angel Face, an advisor to the titular politician. The setting of such works as The Eyes of the Interred and Men of Maize, as well as El Senor Presidente, identify this Central American nation whose most famous native writer is Miguel Asturias.

An American historian with this surname authored several works about the Mormons, such as 1953's Jebediah Smith and the Opening of the West. One device that is described in this work of history is a sachentege, an instrument of torture whose wearer would be unable to sleep, sit or lie down. Name this collection of annals that describes an ethnic group that invaded England during the Norman Conquest.

This book is dedicated to Keith Hudson, a youthful comrade of the author's who died next to him in France. Other chapters in this book examine the themes of homoeroticism and, centrally, of irony as the chief literary legacy of this book's subject. Name this work of criticism about the role played by a certain conflict in the development of Modernist culture, written by Paul Fussell.
The Great War and Modern Memory

This man worked with Carlos Lehder to develop the island of Norman's Cay. In one incident, this character puts on a necklace of eight literal bells and holds onto a sign reading "This is a Star Board" while his friends try their hand at yachting. One punishment handed down by this body was detailed in a work entitled The Work of the Beast. This man's namesake great-grandson wrote the pulp novel that was adapted into the Lon Chaney Sr. Film The Penalty. This man's daughter, the protagonist of the Kathryn Harrison novel Enchantments, was mauled by a bear in Peru, Indiana while working with a circus as a lion tamer. This man did much of the research for one of his books while disguised as a "Major Oughton"; that book later earned him a death threat from the Stern Gang. Tawney in the so-called "storm over the gentry" and, contemporaneously with Eric Hobsbawm, developed the idea of the "general crisis of the 17th century". Low points in this man's career include his declaration that Africa had no history before European colonization and his 1983 "authentication" of the Hitler Diaries, which were later revealed to be a hoax. Name this author of The Last Days of Hitler, a controversial British historian.

Bernard Saisset served under this man and Clement V authorized a posthumous trial of this man, however it was never held. Let's go to press." Thanks to his friendship with J. Edgar Hoover, he this man helped orchestrate the surrender of gangster Lepke Buchalter. The title event occurred on February 4, 1882, as three of the title character's colleagues discover on the opening page. After going to Paris at the age of 25, he studied under Corot, whose influence can be seen on his early works. In 1801, he wrote Thalada the Destroyer, a verse epic set in the Orient, which was followed by Madoc, the story of the South American adventures of the son of the medieval Welsh king Owen Gwyneth. The genesis of this work came in 1899, when the author got lost in the Adirondacks, and wandered around without food for 13 hours. After reading a textbook by Lavoisier (la-vwa-zee-ay), he decided to become a chemist, but his first experimental work was an attempt to disprove Lavoisier's caloric theory of heat. She feels isolated after her governess, Miss Taylor, leaves to marry Mr. Weston. He worked as an engineer at the Howden Airship Works, and integrated his professional work into his writing in works like No Highway and his autobiography, Slide Rule. Willie is sentenced to prison for stabbing a man, and loses both feet from gangrene after being trussed up for three days for attempting to escape. In a short story by Danilo Kis, he flies into the air to prove a point, but then plummets to a grisly death. FTP, name this Austrian, who shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 with Tinbergen and Lorenz, and who is considered a founder of ethology.

He was a poet and was assumed to have written The Contest of Winter and Spring and Farewell to My Cell. FTP, identify this man, who introduced the sung creed, edited the Latin Vulgate, and encouraged study of the liberal arts, as well as the Carolingian miniscule, as abbot of the monastery at Tours and director of the Palace School for Charlemagne.
